dives.title: Cybersecurity Homelab
dives.summary: A seven-VM company-style network on one Proxmox host. I built it so I'd have somewhere to practice attacking and defending something that looks like a real company.

p: I wanted one place where I could run an attack and then check what it looked like from the defender's side. Offense and defense shouldn't be separate worlds. Everything runs on one box: an i7-10900K with 64 GB of RAM and a 2 TB SSD, virtualized with Proxmox.
It's all isolated. Nothing is published to the internet and remote access is Tailscale only. My public notes use placeholders instead of the real address plan.

pfSense sits between the upstream network and the lab segment and handles all the routing, DHCP, DNS and firewalling. The rules are default-deny. The vulnerable boxes get no internet at all, and traffic is only allowed where an exercise needs it.

Security Onion watches a mirrored copy of the lab traffic on a sniffing interface with no IP of its own, so monitoring never changes what it's monitoring. Remote admin goes through Tailscale subnet routing, so I never had to forward a single port.
Stood up Proxmox and carved the network into virtual bridges for the upstream path and the lab segment.
Installed pfSense and wrote the segmentation rules, with DHCP and DNS for the lab.
Built the Windows Server domain controller, created the lab.local domain, OUs, users and groups, then joined a Windows 11 workstation.
Added the Ubuntu box with DVWA and WebGoat in Docker, plus Kali and Metasploitable for controlled testing.
Deployed Security Onion against a span port and confirmed Zeek and Suricata were seeing lab traffic.
Segmentation is the feature. Half of what makes the lab safe is just pfSense refusing traffic that has no reason to exist.
You can't defend what you can't see. Getting the mirror port working so Security Onion actually got traffic taught me more about network monitoring than any reading.
Document as you go and sanitize as you go. Writing public-safe notes made me think about what's an identifier and what's just a concept.

I want to write attack-and-detection walkthroughs with sanitized screenshots, so the detections are backed by real telemetry and not guesses. The attack chain on this site is the scripted version of that.

dives.title: Enterprise IT Support Lab
dives.summary: A Windows domain with a real help-desk ticketing system on top. I built it to practice day-one IT support work: AD, Group Policy, PowerShell, permissions and closing tickets.

p: The homelab is for security. This one is for the support basics underneath it. I built a lab.local domain and set up osTicket so I could work tickets start to finish like a real help desk, and not just click around in Active Directory.

Windows Server runs Active Directory and a Finance SMB share. I used both share-level and NTFS permissions on purpose, so I could see layered access control work the way it does in a real environment.
osTicket runs on Ubuntu with Apache, PHP and MariaDB. It has an IT Support department and public help topics, so every exercise ends in a documented, closed ticket and not a loose note.
A user can sign in and reach the Finance share but gets access denied when they open it. The fix taught me a lot:

Reproduce it from the domain-joined workstation, check the user's AD group membership, find they're missing from Finance-Share-Read, add them with PowerShell, and have them sign out and back in so Windows issues a fresh token.

The sign-out is the whole point. Group membership gets baked into the access token at logon, so adding someone to a group does nothing for their current session. That one detail is behind a lot of 'but I fixed it' tickets.
PowerShell beats clicking. Provisioning a user, placing them in an OU, setting a password and adding them to a group is a few lines, and it's repeatable.
Group Policy is how one change reaches every machine. I used a GPO to map the Finance share as a drive automatically, then validated it with gpupdate and gpresult.
Closing the ticket matters as much as fixing the problem. Writing the resolution in osTicket is the part that makes it support work and not just tinkering.
More ticket scenarios: printer and GPO conflicts, roaming-profile issues and account lockouts. I'll write each one up as a walkthrough you can reproduce.
